about.say: Nineteen years between the interface and the code that ships it.
s: Nineteen years between the interface and the code that ships it.
I am a Product Designer and Front-End Engineer based in Madrid.
who

I studied journalism (Ciencias de la Información) at the Universidad Complutense and then graphic design at Escuela Arteneo — which is probably why my work keeps returning to editorial problems: hierarchy, reading rhythm, and how much meaning survives when a layout gets compressed.
I started in an agency in 2007, building sites for clients like Barceló Viajes and Vodafone.
when who
Then nine years at France Telecom Spain on high-traffic products, optimising flows and conversion structures.
In 2021 I moved fully into design systems at Aliseda, where I created Brickee, their internal system.
when

Since 2023 I have been at Prensa Ibérica working on 42DS: design-token architecture from Figma to Style Dictionary, WCAG 2.1 AA in complex editorial products, and the shared SCSS architecture behind the group's titles.
when numbers why tools
More recently AI has widened that scope.
Rather than treating it as an assistant, I design the context it works inside — the rules, knowledge and governance that keep AI-assisted execution inside a system instead of around it.

section.business-problem.title: Unify without stopping the company.
section.business-problem.say: Prensa Ibérica had grown into a multi-brand ecosystem with different technologies, identities and legacy decisions.
s: Unify without stopping the company.
Prensa Ibérica had grown into a multi-brand ecosystem with different technologies, identities and legacy decisions.
Unification had to happen while BAU work — fixes, sponsorships, visual changes and editorial requests — continued.
So the first job was not “design the new system”.
It was understand the existing one: audit performance and CSS complexity, learn the legacy and identify what could become shared.

section.what-counted.title: One fix, every brand.
section.what-counted.say: The bar was a behaviour rather than a number, and it is worth stating both halves of it.
s: One fix, every brand.
The bar was a behaviour rather than a number, and it is worth stating both halves of it.
What success looked like: A correction made once reaching every title, and a new brand arriving as configuration instead of as code.
If the same fix still had to be repeated per masthead, the system had not done its job whatever it looked like.
What nobody measured: No one wrote that bar down or tracked it against a baseline.
This was business as usual with a system growing inside it, so the evidence is structural — the shared/brand split and the fourteen setups — and not a before-and-after.

That is when a handful of illustrations turns into something worth solving properly, and it is also when it becomes possible to get it wrong at scale.

section.team.title: The set grew because someone kept asking for the next one.
section.team.say: I drew them, but I did not decide when the set needed to grow.
s: The set grew because someone kept asking for the next one.
why
I drew them, but I did not decide when the set needed to grow.
Deborah Garcelán Vargas, then at SPORT, reviewed each illustration with me and told me which one was missing next as communication needs came up.
That is why the seventeen cover the moments they cover: the list was never designed in advance, it was requested one piece at a time.
why
It is also why the grammar could only be written at the end — you cannot extract the rules of a set while the set is still being asked for.

section.what-shaped-them.title: Three limits, and all three are visible in the drawings.
section.what-shaped-them.say: None of them was mine to negotiate, and the set looks the way it looks because of them.
s: Three limits, and all three are visible in the drawings.
None of them was mine to negotiate, and the set looks the way it looks because of them.
why
What I worked inside: SPORT is a photographic newspaper and its palette was already fixed.
The illustration could not compete with the photography for attention, and it could not invent colour to tell one asset apart from another.
What that cost: A quieter register than I would have chosen, and less separation between assets than a free palette would have given me.
They were also drawn around other work rather than in time set aside for them, which puts a ceiling on how far any single one got pushed.

section.grammar.title: Variation comes from scenario. Consistency comes from the visual grammar.
section.grammar.say: I did not decide these four rules and then draw.
s: Variation comes from scenario. Consistency comes from the visual grammar.
I did not decide these four rules and then draw.
I drew, then looked at what the drawings already had in common, and wrote that down.
The order matters more than it sounds: a grammar extracted from work that exists describes something real, while one declared in advance is a wish.
These four are what let a Halloween asset and a failed-process asset belong to the same family.
01 Recognisable silhouette Simple, bold forms keep the asset legible at editorial scale.
numbers
02 Controlled palette Colour reinforces SPORT identity without overwhelming the surrounding UI.
numbers
03 Editorial humour Small narrative gestures make functional moments feel less generic.
numbers
04 Reusable placement Assets can work as standalone illustrations, empty states or contextual support.

A set that holds Euro 2024 and Halloween next to a failed-process state has two different lifespans built into it from the start.
when
The ones tied to a moment have gone.
The ones tied to a permanent product state are the reason the grammar had to exist in the first place: an empty state does not stop being needed.
why
That split is visible in the sheet above once you look for it, and it is the part of the brief nobody writes down.

section.takeaway.title: Systems thinking should make visual expression easier to scale — not flatten it.
section.takeaway.say: The grammar is what makes seventeen assets readable as one set; the scenarios are what keep them from looking like seventeen copies.
